note: Same declared type and affinity. In SQLite INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is an alias for the rowid, so identity needs no AUTOINCREMENT and no GENERATED clause; the seed supplies explicit ids exactly as the PostgreSQL seed does.
Same declared type and affinity. TEXT affinity never converts a number to text, so the storage class of this column is always TEXT.
Same declared type and affinity, nullable in both. NULL is SQLite's own NULL and is reported as JSON null in both dialects.
Same declared type and affinity, nullable in both; the repeated cities the joins lessons rely on are unchanged.

SQLite has no date type. A DATE declaration only selects NUMERIC affinity, and ISO-8601 text is not a numeric literal, so the stored class stays TEXT (measured: typeof(signup_date) = 'text'). This is the column that exercises dynamic typing honestly: declared affinity NUMERIC, stored class TEXT. Compare and format it as text; a host Date object must not be reconstructed from it.
Same declared type and affinity; INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is the rowid alias, and the seed reuses the PostgreSQL ids 1..20.
Same declared type and affinity; the product names are identical to the PostgreSQL seed.
Same declared type and affinity. The repeated categories (Electronics, Home, Outdoor, Kitchen) cover the GROUP BY lessons unchanged.

SQLite has no fixed-scale decimal. NUMERIC affinity stores a value in its smallest lossless class, so the same column reports INTEGER 59 for 59.00 and REAL 42.5 for 42.50 (measured on SQLite 3.31.1): the two-decimal scale is not preserved and the storage class varies per row. TEXT was rejected for exact scale because a TEXT-affinity money column turns `WHERE price > 100` into a lexicographic compare — measured: it returns '59.00' and '9.99'. Display scale with printf('%.2f', price) and keep a result contract's numeric_tolerance at 0 only for values that survive the round trip.
Same declared type and affinity; the zero-stock product 20 (a required edge case) is unchanged.

SQLite has no boolean type. A BOOLEAN declaration selects NUMERIC affinity and the seed stores 1/0 (measured: typeof(active) = 'integer'); TRUE and FALSE are only keywords for 1 and 0. The value is reported as an integer and is never coerced to true/false, so a contract must compare against 1/0. The domain is unenforced: nothing stops an UPDATE setting active = 7.
Same declared type and affinity. The seed keeps the PostgreSQL order ids 1001..1080 untouched, so the joins lessons answer the same questions.

Same declared type and affinity. REFERENCES customers(id) is declared in both, but SQLite does not enforce foreign keys unless the connection sets PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON — the seed only inserts valid ids, so the data satisfies the constraint either way.

SQLite has no timestamp type. TIMESTAMP selects NUMERIC affinity and the seed stores the ISO-8601 text 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM' (measured: typeof(ordered_at) = 'text'). TEXT is deliberate: it is the one text form PostgreSQL prints for a naive timestamp, so a lesson comparing the two dialects sees the same characters. Report it verbatim as a string; never materialise a Date.
Same declared type and affinity. The five status values spread across five months (a required edge case) are unchanged, so the GROUP BY and filter lessons work in both dialects.
Same declared type and affinity; the seed keeps the PostgreSQL ids 1..160.
Same declared type and affinity. As with orders.customer_id, the REFERENCES clause is declared but only enforced when PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON; the seed is internally consistent either way.
Same declared type and affinity. Product 20 is never ordered (a required edge case), so the LEFT JOIN lessons have the same anti-join answer.
Same declared type and affinity. CHECK (quantity > 0) is declared in both and SQLite does enforce CHECK constraints, so the constraint is equally real.

Same divergence as products.price: no fixed scale, and NUMERIC affinity stores the values in the smallest lossless class (measured: typeof(unit_price) IN ('integer','real')). SUM(unit_price) therefore returns a REAL, which is what a money aggregate in this dialect is. The values are identical to the PostgreSQL seed; only the reported representation differs.
Same declared type and affinity. The single row ('commerce', 1) is the dialect's marker that it seeded the same dataset_version; a host that supports more than one dataset would add rows here.
Same declared type and affinity. dataset_version 1 is shared by schema.sql, schema.sqlite.sql and both seeds; the audit reads it from each file rather than trusting this note.
